In Dagara and Lobi tradition the gyil balafon is often played in pairs with kuor drum accompaniment, and is also used in funeral duets. Cameroon has the komemchang orchestra of six balafons of different sizes, and bar bands of three to five balafons with percussion; Bikusi folk songs are also accompanied by balafon, shakers and drums. Since the 1980s, in African roots music and world music, the Rail Band led by Salif Keita and the Mandinka guitar music of eastern Guinea have carried its style on.

The balafon is the gourd-resonated xylophone of West Africa, a struck idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.212. The keys, usually seventeen to twenty-one of them, are fixed on a wooden frame or freely laid out, and beneath them hang gourd resonators of graded size whose holes are covered with a membrane that produces a nasal buzz. The player usually sits on a low stool or stands, striking with two rubber-headed mallets. It is used by peoples such as the Mande, Bwaba, Bobo, Senufo and Gur, and appears in solo playing, ritual, festivals, funerals and weddings, and at court; it is often played in ensembles of low, middle and high instruments.
巴拉風為以木鍵敲擊的體鳴樂器，鍵下懸掛大小漸變的葫蘆共鳴器，共鳴器小孔覆膜，產生: The balafon is an idiophone struck on wooden keys, with gourd resonators of graded size hung beneath them; small holes in the resonators are covered with membrane, which gives a nasal, buzzing timbre. It commonly has seventeen to twenty-one keys and can play eighteen to twenty-one notes, and instruments with fewer keys also exist; the tuning may be four-, five- or seven-note. It is played with two mallets, and the size of the resonating gourds affects the volume: the large balafon has long keys and large gourds and a lower range, while the small balani has short keys and small gourds and a higher range. Compared with other instruments of the xylophone family, its distinguishing feature is the membrane-covered resonator.
巴拉風的木條傳統以科索玫瑰木製成，慢火乾燥後削底調音；gyil則用利加硬木。固定: The bars are traditionally made of kosso rosewood, dried over a slow fire and shaved underneath to tune them; the gyil uses liga hardwood. On a fixed-key instrument a wooden frame carries the bars, which are suspended on leather straps, with gourd resonators of gradually changing size hung beneath. The small holes of the resonators are covered with the silk membrane of spider egg cases, and today also with cigarette paper or plastic film; the gyil covers the holes with spider silk held by antelope sinew and leather. The mallets are wooden with rubber-wound heads. The materials of the remaining parts are not recorded.
巴拉風起源至少可追溯至12世紀，口述歷史與馬里帝國興起相連。1352年，Ibn: The balafon can be traced back at least to the twelfth century, and oral history links it to the rise of the Mali Empire. In 1352 Ibn Battuta recorded that a balafon was already at the court of the Mali ruler Mansa Suleyman. European visitors of the seventeenth century described an instrument already close to the modern form. The Atlantic slave trade carried players to the Americas, and in 1776 the Virginia Gazette records African Americans playing the barrafoo, though the records of it in North America disappear by the middle of the nineteenth century. After the 1980s the balafon revived with the growth of African roots music and world music; the Rail Band was led by Salif Keita, and the Maninka of eastern Guinea also carried balafon playing into guitar music.
巴拉風通常以兩支包橡膠或樹膠的琴槌敲擊木鍵發聲。固定鍵型可坐於矮凳演奏，也可用肩: The balafon is normally sounded by striking the wooden keys with two mallets wound with rubber or tree gum. A fixed-key instrument can be played sitting on a low stool, or the frame can be hung from a shoulder strap or belt so that the player stands. A beginner can start on a free-key or pit balafon, the keys laid out separately on a soft surface, and then gradually get used to striking many keys. In some traditions one player works several keys with two mallets, while in others two or more players share a single keyboard.
